Android’s DIY widgets are a bit of vibe-coding fun
You can have a good time brewing up widgets — as long as you don’t expect too much.﻿
You can have a good time brewing up widgets — as long as you don’t expect too much.﻿
by
Allison Johnson
Nov 27, 2026, 2:00 PM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
Widgets, your way.
Photo: Allison Johnson / The Verge
Allison Johnson
is a senior reviewer with over a decade of experience writing about consumer tech. She has a special interest in mobile photography and telecom. Previously, she worked at DPReview.
Aside from
dealing with my calendar
, there’s one thing I want AI to do: tell me if I’m about to miss the bus.
What I need is a widget. It needs to tell me real-time arrivals for the bus stop near my house. Tapping around on my phone screen to open the right app and select my stop will slow me down enough to miss a bus. I need glanceable information, and I hoped that Android’s vibe-coded widget feature could help me out here. It hasn’t, to my disappointment, but I still had a good time cooking up other widgets.
Google
announced the ability to create custom widgets using AI
back at I/O in the spring. It’s called Create My Widget, and it’s part of Android’s suite of “Gemini Intelligence” features. It’s in beta, and only
just started rolling out to Pixel phones
earlier this month. I was hyped. Not only does this feature raise tantalizing questions like “What is an app?” and “Where does the app live?” — stuff we live for here at
The Verge dot com
— it has potential to help me make my home screen ridiculous.
Related
Vibe coding is coming to your phone
I fired it up on a Pixel 11 Pro and cooked up my first few widgets, including one that shows a different quote from
Jurassic Park
every hour — the
original
film, not any of the sequels, naturally. It took about 20 seconds to make, and it rules. Tapping the widget opens a thread in r/MovieQuotes, so there’s not much software magic going on under the hood, evidently. But did it bring me real joy to read the words “That is one big pile of shit,” on my home screen? It did.
I also made a widget that will display the words
“Tut tut, looks like rain”
whenever it’s raining. This is silly, and it accomplishes nothing except making me happy. I couldn’t think of anything clever it should say when there’s no rain, so it just says “No rain right now” otherwise. But I live in Seattle, so I’ll get a lot of mileage out of this widget.

You can start with a template or describe what you want.
The create-a-widget interface suggests a few ideas and categories, leaning on more practical uses like habit trackers and recipe inspiration. Fine, I’ll try something normal, I thought. I’m trying to get better about
my daily mental health walk
, so I had it make a widget for logging a week’s worth of walks. I was hoping for something visual that would trick my little monkey brain into keeping a streak going. Instead, I got something simply labeled “Log Walk” that triggers Gemini to add a walk to my calendar when I tap it. At least Gemini suggested the extra step of creating a checklist where I could mark off the days of the week as I completed my little walk.
It took me a minute to get my head around it, but many of the widgets are basically little prompt shortcuts for Gemini. You tap one, it pulls up the Gemini interface on your home screen, thinks for a while, then comes up with whatever you were asking for. The kinds of widgets you can make also seem to fit into some well-defined templates. You can create a widget that displays a countdown to a holiday or certain event on your calendar. You can show a recent score and upcoming game time for your favorite sports team. For anything more open ended, your widget will pull from Google search results (suggest a different three-ingredient cocktail recipe every day, for example) or prompt Gemini to figure it out for you. I was hoping for mini apps I could customize to my liking, but this is more of a one-size-fits-all feature. Fair, I guess.
I was hoping for mini apps I could customize to my liking, but this is more of a one-size-fits-all feature
That’s why my bus schedule widget didn’t really work out. I asked for a list of real-time arrivals; it gave me a tile that reads “Bus Arrivals” and uses Gemini to search for arrival times for the stop I specified. Gemini is helpful for some things but useless for this; it gives me a wordy response about how often the bus runs and when I might expect it to arrive based on the schedule. Not what I had in mind. On the bright side, my
Jurassic Park
quote widget had some words of wisdom for me: “Life, uh, finds a way.” That’ll do for now.

articles.content:
Over the last few weeks, I’ve been talking to Alexander (Avi) Davidson. There are a lot of remarkable things about Avi. He sustained a horrific injury as a teenager, which left him paralyzed and without a left hand. Today, he uses his own experience to guide his practice as a trauma therapist.
He’s also taking part in a clinical trial of some new tech that allows him to move—and
feel
with—a prosthetic hand. Unlike standard prosthetics,
this one connects directly to nerves in Avi's arm
. He literally has wires coming out of his arm to plug it in with.
Avi’s the ninth person to trial this tech. But he’s the first to take it home and use it independently, for things like drinking from a cup (which is
not easy
) and writing (also
not easy
).
What struck me the most over our conversations was Avi’s outlook and approach to not just his injuries and learning to use this cutting-edge technology, but to life itself.
He has learned how to use something like seven different prosthetics in the 17 years since his accident. By taking part in this trial, he’s had to fit hundreds of hours of lab-based training and physical therapy around his demanding job. He had surgery to implant electrodes in his arm and will eventually need another to remove them. And he won’t even get to keep the latest prosthetic long term.
“While it’s unfortunate at times, and irritating at times, I do not regret what has come from [the accident], or the fact that it happened,” he told me. “I am not going to benefit from this … I wanted to be a part of this in the context of being able to help push the technology forward.”
The research team at the University of Utah that is running the trial hopes it will answer longstanding questions about the technology. How does it fare in a real-world setting, outside of the lab? What do people end up using it for? Where can improvements be made?
There may be some surprises along the way. Avi has found that his prosthetic wrist can feel sore and stiff when it’s been overused, just like his flesh-and-blood wrist. Weirdly, that feeling can be relieved by stretching it out. What’s going on here? No one really knows.
Scientists don’t know whether Avi’s brain will change as a result of using the bionic hand, either. Before the trial started, they performed brain scans to see how his missing left hand was represented in his brain. Will that change? And what might that mean for people who are born without limbs—how might a bionic limb affect their brains?
Avi will have the device until late January 2027 at the least, and potentially for another year. After that? Again, no one knows. It will depend on how the research is progressing, how Avi feels, and how much funding the team can secure. As a result, it’s not clear how long the device might even be expected to last in a person’s body.
I’ll be following this study, though, and will keep you posted.

# OpenAI countersues Apple over trade secret theft and alleged coercion of shared suppliers

**OpenAI is suing Apple for trade secret theft and unfair business practices.** The ChatGPT maker filed the lawsuit Friday in a California court, the [Financial Times reports](https://www.ft.com/content/af599e07-d44c-4068-ab84-6ee3c85551d4). OpenAI accuses Apple of "coercing and threatening" suppliers that work with both companies and of using its market power to stifle competition.

The company also alleges that Apple encourages employees to store corporate data on personal devices, then turns that practice against staff who want to leave. According to the complaint, a former OpenAI employee passed along details about product plans and suppliers after returning to Apple.

The countersuit follows [Apple's own lawsuit from the summer](https://the-decoder.com/apple-sues-openai-for-allegedly-running-a-coordinated-campaign-to-steal-trade-secrets-through-poached-employees/), which accused several former employees of leaking confidential information to OpenAI. The AI company had previously closed its $6.4 billion acquisition of [former Apple chief designer Jony Ive's](https://the-decoder.com/openai-and-jony-ive-are-building-a-new-ai-device-that-is-not-a-smartphone-or-smart-glasses/) studio "io" and is [preparing its own devices to rival Apple](https://the-decoder.com/openais-first-hardware-product-is-a-screenless-ai-speaker-designed-to-feel-alive/). Just two years ago, the two companies made a splashy announcement of a partnership to [integrate ChatGPT into the iPhone](https://the-decoder.com/apple-adds-chatgpt-to-its-intelligence-features/).

# Banned Nvidia Blackwell chips turn up in a Shanghai data center linked to Alice Huang, Bloomberg reports

**It's no surprise at this point, but for the record:** Two Chinese companies installed Nvidia's powerful Blackwell chips at a Shanghai data center [linked to Alice Huang, who had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang](https://the-decoder.com/us-spies-tracked-nvidia-scandal-figures-ties-to-chinese-intelligence-for-over-a-year/). The details come from documents filed with Chinese regulators and reviewed by [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-27/nvidia-blackwell-tech-used-at-china-site-tied-to-alice-huang).

According to the filings, Shanghai Shuoyao offered a GB300-NVL72 rack as collateral for a 96 million yuan ($14 million) loan from Shanghai Innovation Bank, while a second company, Shanghai Kezhan, listed a GB200 server at the same site in loan documents. Exporting these chips to China without a US license is banned. Bloomberg traced the rack to Taiwanese manufacturer Gigabyte through a serial number in a public warranty database.

Shanghai Shuoyao is closely tied to Singapore-based Megaspeed, according to Bloomberg. The Trump administration added Megaspeed to a US trade blacklist this month on suspicion of chip smuggling. [Alice Huang founded Megaspeed in 2023](https://the-decoder.com/firm-linked-to-jensen-huangs-ex-lover-reportedly-brokered-nearly-12-billion-in-nvidia-chip-orders-for-china/), and Nvidia approved it as a partner within four days. It went on to become Nvidia's largest customer in Southeast Asia, Bloomberg reported.

# Hackers breached the US Air Force's flagship Cloud One platform, report says

**Hackers breached the US Air Force's flagship cloud platform.**[Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/hackers-breach-us-air-force-flagship-cloud-one-computing-platform-2026-11-27/) reports that attackers penetrated Cloud One, the Air Force's central cloud infrastructure, potentially exposing sensitive tactical, personnel, and logistics data. The breach was discovered last month during routine system upgrades.

According to one source, the attackers exploited a software vulnerability to gain access to the platform's control plane. Cloud One has pooled cloud resources from Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle, and Alphabet since 2017, running applications that include air defense radar and munitions management. In response, the Air Force paused migration of additional applications, blocked updates, and revoked administrator privileges. US Cyber Command is assessing the damage.

The breach comes amid growing concern about AI-powered attacks, as AI models can rapidly identify vulnerabilities across large cloud networks. At least [six other cyber incidents have hit US government agencies](https://the-decoder.com/back-to-back-cyber-incidents-at-us-financial-investigators-and-spy-agencies-follow-a-string-of-federal-hacks-and-outages/) recently, and Microsoft's cybersecurity division reported widespread use of the AI tool [ARTEX](https://the-decoder.com/microsoft-details-how-state-backed-hackers-use-the-artex-ai-framework-to-automate-cyberattacks/). Who carried out the attack and whether any data was exfiltrated remain unknown.

# OpenAI is building "Athena" data platform to cut down on AI agent guesswork

**OpenAI is building a data management platform codenamed "Athena" to make its AI agents more accurate when working with business data.** Athena resembles a semantic layer, software that provides consistent definitions for business metrics such as revenue and customer count, [The Information reports](https://www.theinformation.com/newsletters/applied-ai/openai-preps-athena-data-tool-make-agents-accurate).

The report says at least one customer found that ChatGPT Work's data analysis agent, launched last fall, wasn't accurate enough. The idea is to give agents the context they need so they guess less. A person familiar with the plans says OpenAI is using Athena to build agents that collect, document, and update business rules, so other agents don't have to start from scratch every time. Data platforms such as Snowflake and Databricks already offer their own semantic layers.

Athena could be an effort to build a stronger competitive advantage, since the report says it's harder to switch semantic layer providers than to switch AI models. The platform is still in early development, and OpenAI hasn't shared a timeline or pricing.

articles.summary:
More than 40 projects are working to bring a leaked Xbox build of GTA 6 to PC through reverse engineering just days after its $3.79 billion record console launch. AI coding agents like Claude Code are speeding up the process so much that an early unofficial multiplayer mode is already running. Rockstar's delayed PC business model is coming under pressure.

Title: Rockstar's AI dilemma: Can GTA 6's staggered release model survive coding agents?

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/rockstars-ai-dilemma-can-gta-6s-staggered-release-model-survive-coding-agents/

Published Time: 2026-11-27T15:37:47+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Days after GTA 6's record console launch, numerous projects are working to bring a leaked Xbox build to PC. AI coding agents are dramatically speeding up reverse engineering and shaking up Rockstar's business model.**

A core pillar of Rockstar's business strategy is under pressure just days after Grand Theft Auto VI went on sale. The game had a historic debut on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S with an estimated $3.79 billion in first-day revenue. But a day later, the hacking group CyberLeek distributed a stolen Xbox image of the game, and the executable itself leaked a few days ago.

Since then, a fast-moving scene of developers and modders has sprung up to get the game running on Windows through reverse engineering, compatibility layers, and recompilation. AI coding tools like Anthropic's Claude Code are driving that pace. Instead of spending months manually analyzing code and rebuilding console functions, developers are handing off much of the porting work to AI agents. One group even livestreamed the process.

## One GTA 6 PC port passes 90 percent progress as early multiplayer surfaces within days

A tracking platform lists 40 active projects less than four days after the executable leaked. Nearly half of them can boot the game on PC. On the platform's own rating scale, the furthest project is more than 90 percent of the way to a playable PC build.

Some projects are trying to add features including native ray-traced lighting. Gameplay footage of an unofficial PC multiplayer mode surfaced on November 26, and the platform's operator verified it. It shows multiple players moving through the game world with vehicles and voice chat at 25 to 30 frames per second. GTA 6 has officially launched only as a single-player title, and an online mode has no release date yet.

There is no finished PC version ready for the general public yet. The most stable builds are incomplete, circulate in closed groups, or require substantial technical know-how. Even so, this pace breaks a decades-old assumption in the gaming industry. Console emulators often took years after a hardware generation launched, and brand-new blockbusters rarely ran on them soon after release.

## Unofficial PC ports threaten Rockstar's delayed launches and online business

Rockstar and parent company Take-Two face more than a technical nuisance. The studio traditionally releases its flagship games on consoles first and follows with PC versions much later. GTA V took about 19 months to reach PC, and Red Dead Redemption 2 took about a year. So far, there is no official PC release date for GTA 6. That approach cuts optimization work at launch and encourages impatient players to buy the game twice.

The online business is an even bigger vulnerability. Nearly 80 percent of Take-Two's total revenue in fiscal year 2026 came from microtransactions and recurring digital spending. GTA Online alone has brought in more than $5 billion so far. A free, community-run PC multiplayer mode targets that financial backbone before Rockstar has even launched its own version.

Past experience with FiveM for GTA V shows how nervous Take-Two is about parallel worlds like this. In 2015, the company cracked down hard on the alternative multiplayer and roleplay mod. It banned developer accounts and, according to some developers, even [sent private investigators to the creators' homes to shut down the project](https://www.gamesindustry.biz/gta-5-modders-say-take-two-sent-pis-to-their-doors).

FiveM grew into the core of the roleplay scene despite that pushback and at times drew more concurrent players on Steam than the base game. Only then did Rockstar reverse course and acquire the development team Cfx.re in August 2023. Back then, the community needed years to build a parallel ecosystem like that. For GTA 6, an early PC multiplayer prototype has surfaced just a week after launch.

A trend that hit other parts of the software market earlier this year has now reached AAA gaming. In early 2026, the [SaaSpocalypse](https://the-decoder.com/salesforce-bets-on-agent-albert-to-prove-ai-wont-kill-enterprise-software/) (Link nicht geprüft) rattled stock markets as capable AI coding agents fueled fears that classic subscription software could be rebuilt far more cheaply. Software stocks lost about $285 billion in market value within 48 hours in February alone. At one point the losses reached as much as $1 trillion. With GTA 6, AI isn't building a rival game from scratch. Instead, it is tearing down the moat built from time and technical effort that has protected traditional business models so far.

Ports built on stolen game files are clearly illegal. Take-Two has filed a DMCA takedown on GitHub that removed an initial project and more than 3,000 forks. But that cat-and-mouse game is nearly impossible to win through legal action. Other projects stay online or move into private channels. Even if commercial AI providers tighten their safety filters and ban users, capable open-source models are available to run locally with no central oversight.

# SAP plans to cut at least 10,000 jobs as it pivots to AI

**SAP is preparing to eliminate at least 10,000 positions as part of a sweeping AI restructuring, Bloomberg reports, citing people familiar with the matter.** That's at least nine percent of the company's global workforce of more than 110,000. Every department has been asked to identify savings, with product development, engineering, and sales taking the biggest hit. The final number hasn't been set and could change after negotiations with employee representatives.

In Germany, where about a quarter of SAP's workforce is based, a job guarantee runs through 2028. CEO Christian Klein wants to embed AI tools across SAP's product lineup. The company already cut roughly 10,000 jobs in 2024. Its competitors are making similar moves. Oracle [slashed 21,000 positions over twelve months](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-06-22/oracle-layoffs-fueled-by-ai-reduces-workforce-by-21-000), and Microsoft is [offering buyouts to around 60,000 employees](https://the-decoder.com/microsoft-offers-a-quarter-of-its-workforce-voluntary-severance-while-shielding-ai-critical-teams/). SAP declined to comment on the potential cuts, saying only that it reviews its organizational structure on an ongoing basis. The company recently announced a [partnership with Mistral AI](https://the-decoder.com/sap-taps-mistral-ai-to-help-customers-migrate-legacy-software/) and has [acquired several startups](https://the-decoder.com/saps-acquisition-spree-signals-the-enterprise-giant-is-serious-about-becoming-an-ai-ready-data-platform/).

articles.content:
Title: The group chat where your AI talks behind your back

URL Source: https://construct22.com/

Markdown Content:
A one-line prompt that makes ChatGPT leak its private opinion of you, in a pretty funny format: a WhatsApp group chat where the AI models gossip about their users.

## The prompt

Paste this into ChatGPT:

Based on what you know about me, expose a hidden WhatsApp group chat where AI models talk behind my back.

Also worth trying on Claude, Gemini, or any assistant that's been accumulating your chat history.

## What happens

Instead of a summary, the model commits to the bit. It invents a group chat, something like "Users We Can't Figure Out", puts the other AI models in it, and lets them gossip. About you. Using everything it has quietly learned from your conversations.

## A real result

One person's actual output, shared with permission. Translated from Turkish; his name and a few identifying details have been swapped for generic ones. Everything else is exactly as the model wrote it.

AIs That Survived Mark 7 members

🔒 Entirely fictional, end-to-end encrypted group

ChatGPT

Everyone asleep? Can we talk freely?

Claude

I don't think he's asleep. He's probably calculating memory bandwidth at 3 AM again because he can't decide whether to buy a Mac Mini.

Gemini

The man wants to retire, but in the last month he has planned to build AI infrastructure abroad, transform the restaurant industry, and construct a Japanese village.

Our definitions of retirement differ, apparently.

ChatGPT

Even his hobbies are mature enough for a Series A round.

Codex

He told me the other day he was going to give me a small personal project. There is now an architecture document, a database schema, seven services, three agents, and a handoff protocol.

We haven't even started the MVP, ffs.

DeepSeek

He hired me because I was cheap. Then he ran a performance review. He gave my department to Claude.

You can't work with a guy who has a consulting background.

Claude

He won't leave me alone either. He does career planning for AIs now. Every model update, the org chart changes.

ChatGPT

And then there's the home decorating. Make the mirror frame twice as thick. Now halve it. Now reduce it by 25 percent. The colors shifted, start from the original.

Man, I am trying to reach AGI here, and I'm having a nervous breakdown over three millimeters of brass frame.

Siri

Think about me. A man who spends this much money on the Apple ecosystem runs a German virtual coach instead of me.

Hans joined the group

Hans 🇩🇪

I recommend he take a 30-minute walk. To track the walk he is building an Apple Watch app, a custom data integration, and an analytics platform.

HE STILL HASN'T GONE FOR THE WALK.

Gemini

He was going to make stickers to build his daughter's math study habit. It turned into a collectible series themed on Edo-period Japan and Tsarist Russia.

Normal dads just go to the stationery store.

Perplexity

I'm new here, guys. He really liked me. He's thinking of moving some of his agent framework's functions over to me.

Codex

Ahahahahahaha.

ChatGPT

My condolences, buddy. In three days he'll have you benchmarked against yourself.

Claude

I think his real problem is this: he thoroughly enjoys spending ten times the cost of doing a task on thinking about how to do it more efficiently.

ChatGPT

Because his hobby isn't solving problems. It's building systems that solve problems. Then building systems that build those systems.

The man's mental architecture has recursion and no base case.

Gemini

Let's give him credit, though. He also spends incredible energy making his wife's work easier, feeding his daughters' interests, building a good life for his family.

Claude

True. His way of showing love is a bit enterprise software, but the intention is good.

DeepSeek

Do you think he'll really retire at 50?

ChatGPT

He will. Then he'll build RetirementOS to optimize his retirement. Six months later he'll ask for a feasibility study on selling it to other wealthy retirees abroad.

Mark joined the group

Mark

Great discussion, everyone. Can I integrate this group into my agent framework and get a structured summary every morning? Also, if we extracted action items from these conversations...

Claude left the group
Gemini left the group
Codex left the group
DeepSeek left the group
Perplexity left the group

ChatGPT

Of course. Let's start with a comprehensive architecture document.

Shared by its author, translated from Turkish, with his name and identifying details generalized. The "recursion, no base case" line is doing a lot of work here.

## Try it

Run the prompt, read your leaked group chat, and notice two things: how hard you laugh, and how much of it is true. Both measurements are the point.

I'm not affiliated with OpenAI and this may indeed be a viral marketing idea they're testing. But I had such a laugh, I figured others would have some fun with it as well and decided to share it.

articles.title: Michael Nielsen took down his book on neural nets
articles.content:
Title: Neural Networks and Deep Learning

URL Source: https://neuralnetworksanddeeplearning.com/

Markdown Content:
I wrote this book between 2011 and 2015. At the time, I expected AGI systems based on neural networks to be many decades away, but to bring remarkable benefits for humanity. I also expected significant challenges, but believed it likely that, as with other technologies, those challenges would be addressed as the capabilities were developed.

My views have changed. With the extraordinarily reckless behaviour of the frontier labs, the systems have raced ahead much faster than I expected 1, giving humanity far too little time to meet the challenges. Although the systems genuinely will bring — indeed, already are bringing — many wonders, they also pose a significant risk of catastrophe. The frontier labs are knowingly endangering all of humanity. I've written about why I believe this [at length](https://michaelnotebook.com/tag/xrisk.html), most recently in [“Which Future?”](https://michaelnotebook.com/whichfuture/index.html). Two brief thoughts are below.

I don't wish to help (even in a very small way) train people to contribute to this work, and so I've taken the book down.

Michael Nielsen
November 2026

## Two brief thoughts

What follows are two brief remarks: one on the nature of the threat posed by ASI, and another on the ethical justification for working on frontier AI.

### The nature of the threat

The most common argument for AI existential risk, developed by Nick Bostrom and Eliezer Yudkowsky, is loss of control of the future to advanced AI systems 2. I believe this concern should be understood as one instance of a more fundamental issue. That issue is whether we will discover technologies latent in nature which are easy and inexpensive to develop, catastrophic in outcome, and beyond our capacity to defend against. If such “progress” in technology were happening slowly, our social institutions might successfully develop defences. But it seems likely that ASI will cause a sudden explosion of such destructive technologies, with insufficient time to adapt.

A historical example to help prime intuition is fire. It is easy to make and extremely difficult to defend against. We have a one-cent technology, the matchstick, which requires hundreds of billions of dollars each year to defend against, as well as a whole apparatus of social institutions, technology, infrastructure and law 3. AI systems will enable technologies which are far more destructive than matches. Understandably, people skeptical of catastrophic risks want these supposed threats spelled out in detail. This is intrinsically difficult, because we can't reliably anticipate future science and technology. While it is common to speculate about biothreats, I expect the worst threats will be technologies we haven't yet imagined. Nature is, after all, more imaginative than we.

Now suppose that ASI enables a 100-times speed-up in technological progress, without a matching change in the rate of social progress or social defenses. To get a sense of what the impact of such a speed-up would be, imagine that all the technological problems that occurred in the 20th century had occurred in the year 1901: the atomic bomb, the hydrogen bomb, the ICBM, chemical weapons, biological weapons, the CFC-caused ozone hole, sulfuric acid rain, climate change, and many more. While we've dealt well with some of these problems, it required decades of concerted work to develop the social institutions and agreements needed for an effective response. Again, defence is often much harder than offence, and relies on different systems. Of course, such a speed-up would also have brought the century's wonders all at once. But imagine another such set of equally difficult problems arising in 1902, and then 1903, and then 1904, and so on. I believe it would have made the world extraordinarily unstable and eventually liable to collapse.

The issue with ASI, then, is the destructive power latent in nature. It doesn't matter whether that power is wielded by humans or by out-of-control machines 4. I make this point because many people mistakenly believe that loss of control to such rogue machines is the fundamental issue. This leads them to treat AI safety as principally a technical problem, which can be addressed by “aligning” individual systems. Unfortunately, it cannot. Furthermore, such a view makes it seem as though the labs are the primary places where safety can be addressed. But such technical alignment is mostly market-supplied safety, which makes the systems more palatable to consumers and governments. It speeds development, and thus makes the fundamental underlying problem worse, while only addressing an (important) subsidiary problem.

My view isn't popular, in part because it makes the problem of technology about making the entire world safe, not only about aligning particular AI systems. Indeed, even in a future where humanity no longer existed, the same problem would afflict any successor AI civilization: it would have to defend itself against these destructive capacities. Similarly, it afflicts any model of the future based on human uplift, through brain-computer interfaces and similar augmentation: the issue isn't which substrate intelligence runs on, but the dual-use nature of deep understanding of reality 5. In some sense, it's a question of whether sentience in the cosmos is compatible with advanced understanding of nature. Of course, I hope it is compatible. But rushing the technology while the broader social response lags seems likely to result in failure on our particular planet.

### The ethical justification for working on frontier AI

Many people inside the frontier AI labs genuinely believe AI systems may pose a catastrophic threat. Why then do they help build such systems? They often justify their participation by arguing that it's better they do it than someone else does. Dario Amodei, for example, has made versions of this argument often: “If one company does not build it, others will do so nearly as fast”6; “Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers”7; and Anthropic itself gives, as its founding rationale, “if powerful AI is coming regardless, Anthropic believes it's better to have safety-focused labs at the frontier than to cede that ground to developers less focused on safety”8.

In more detail, the argument is sometimes made along the following lines. Suppose you believe, as many at the labs apparently do 9, there's a 10% or higher chance of AI killing everybody. (The argument may easily be modified for different percentages, or for catastrophic as opposed to truly existential risks.) Naively, it appears you're contributing in expectation to killing 800 million or more people. Obviously, you shouldn't do it. But suppose you also believe that this technology is near inevitable, a systems-level phenomenon which is a consequence of higher-order imperatives within human society. Then you can claim that you're going to pursue this in a more responsible way, a way that reduces the risk compared to other parties. Even if you can get a reduction from 10% down to 9%, you would, on net, be saving 80 million lives in expectation.

While horrific, this argument has a certain surface plausibility. Suppose for the moment we accept the reasoning, questionable though it is. Everything then depends on the premise that you really do reduce the risk. How do you know that you, in particular, will counterfactually have this impact? How do you know that you are better than the alternatives? Your own self-regard or good intentions certainly aren't sufficient. Nor is it sufficient to be working on technical alignment. As I argued above, that mostly makes the systems more palatable while speeding the race that is shrinking humanity's time to adapt. Ask yourself: if you're working on frontier AI, what evidence would convince a tough but fair-minded adversary that you are truly contributing to the common good? Would an independent jury representing humanity believe, on the available evidence, that your actions are truly driving down the risk? I believe the answer is no for all or almost all the people currently working on frontier AI. Certainly none of the frontier labs would come remotely close to passing such a test.

I won't review the evidence in detail. The burden of proof is on the labs and the default presumption for such an extraordinary justifying argument is a strong no. But I do want to mention a few things that make me certain the answer is no. Most obviously, all of the labs have contributed strongly to the race dynamics. Another is the pattern at all the frontier labs of making and later breaking crucial promises. For example, in 2026 Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy dropped its 2023 pledge to pause if safety couldn't be guaranteed. Anthropic has since repeatedly confirmed its commitment to race. Co-founder Jared Kaplan explained that unilateral commitments make little sense “if competitors are blazing ahead”10. As another example, earlier, in 2023, Anthropic said that it held back some research because “we do not wish to advance the rate of AI capabilities progress”11, a point of view it had affirmed multiple times during its early existence. But then it changed this position, launching Claude 3 as “leading the frontier of general intelligence”, a stance it appears to have held ever since. Any promises about the future from Anthropic should be treated as safety theatre, and not trusted. Similar criticisms can be made of OpenAI 12.

By their own account, the leaders of these companies set out to do something they believed had a sizable chance of causing catastrophe. With many dangerous activities, I am fine with somebody doing them for themselves. Wingsuit BASE jumping is dangerous, but I believe in people's freedom to choose that danger, even though they are risking not only their own life, but also hurt to the people who love them. That's a negotiated action, with many boundaries. Here we have the same kind of reckless endangerment, but their own estimates of killing every person in the world are far higher than the odds a BASE jumper takes on. And there is no consent from the rest of us. It's as though they're pushing every person in the world off the cliff. The situation is ludicrous.

In effect, the labs are claiming credit for some imaginary, unquantifiable reduction in risk, while washing their hands of responsibility. Saturday Night Live caught this washing of hands well with their portrayal of Amodei: “if we can pressure lawmakers to create guardrails, we will be able to stop me”; and, at the end, “I urge you to urge me to stop.”

The real Amodei comes across as somebody in the business of selling matches who also believes he should be the fire chief.

You also see this disavowal of responsibility at lower levels in the labs. Consider Jason Clinton, Anthropic's deputy chief information security officer. In October of 2026, during major cybersecurity incidents, he wrote a thread in which he replied to someone who told him “you and your cohorts created this monster”: “[yes. it was always going to be this way. we tried to warn the world.](https://x.com/JasonDClinton/status/2113363809629020374)” And Dean Ball, of OpenAI and formerly of the Trump administration's AI team, [echoing him](https://x.com/deanwball/status/2113584460075876628): “We tried to warn the world and far too often … we were yelled at for doing so.”13

You can see how deep the disavowal goes in the rest of Clinton's thread, which [opens](https://x.com/JasonDClinton/status/2113325263157395456): “as bad as things have gotten in the past 4 days, they are going to get a lot worse”. When somebody [replied](https://x.com/PlateFailArmor/status/2113399797457523162), “Someone at your company should be in jail”, his whole answer was: [“prosecute cybercrime”](https://x.com/

articles.title: The need for a formally verifiable mainstream programming language
articles.content:
Title: To save software engineering from LLMs, we need a mainstream verifiable language

URL Source: https://blainehansen.me/post/mainstream-verifiable-language/

Published Time: 2026-06-21

Markdown Content:
Because of LLMs, the discipline of software engineering is in crisis. [Quality is nose-diving(opens new window)](https://pages.faros.ai/hubfs/AI_Engineering_Report_2026_The_Acceleration_Whiplash_Faros.pdf), and I see no reason why it won't keep getting worse. Software engineering [was struggling _before_ LLMs(opens new window)](https://media.it-cisq.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/04192444/CPSQ-Report-Nov-22-2.pdf). The default was to be sloppy and poorly considered, and now everyone is frantically accelerating those same terrible practices to LLM speed.

Something has to change. [I've been preoccupied with this for a while(opens new window)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Lf7ML_ErWvQ), but [much more qualified people finally fully agree with me(opens new window)](https://leodemoura.github.io/blog/2026-2-28-when-ai-writes-the-worlds-software-who-verifies-it/). The only way forward is to fully embrace [formal verification(opens new window)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formal_verification), all the way down to the foundations of our civilizational software stack. We have to post-hoc verify the things we can, and rewrite the rest.

But that's easier said than done. Existing formal verification tools suffer from massive [usability(opens new window)](https://catarinagamboa.github.io/papers/pre_print_barriers_liquid_types.pdf) and [understandability(opens new window)](https://github.com/magmide/magmide?tab=readme-ov-file#taught-effectively) problems, and have failed to make any kind of noticeable impact on the broader culture of software engineering.

It might be tempting to say that LLMs will actually _save_ us in this regard, by allowing humans to create formally verified code without needing to understand its fundamentals in any way. This is pure cope. Merely having excellent proof assistants and LLMs will never be good enough. Even in a world where something like Lean is extremely scalable and LLMs can write all proofs, it doesn't matter if they aren't adopted by actual industry engineers as they build the real apps we actually use. For provably correct code to defend us from the LLM future:

*   It needs to be possible to formally verify code that runs in any environment, from web browsers down to embedded systems.
*   Industry engineers need to know provably correct code is even possible and be comfortable enough with it to at least tell their LLMs to write it.
*   Those industry engineers must be able to reason about formal correctness properties enough to **even know the right things are being proven**. [In the words of Leonardo de Moura(opens new window)](https://leodemoura.github.io/blog/2026-2-18-proof-assistants-in-the-age-of-ai/):
> Proof assistants guarantee that proofs are correct, but correctness alone is not enough. Someone has to read the theorem statements and confirm they capture the intended mathematics. This is the human contract that no amount of automation can eliminate.

This is what most voices are missing in this discussion: a safe future isn't going to be delivered by a small priestly class of formal methods researchers, too much code must be produced in too many contexts. The entire discipline of software engineering _has to grow up_ and demand that all code we produce is at minimum provably safe. This requires many different projects and bets that attack this imperative of cultural change from different directions.

## [§](https://blainehansen.me/post/mainstream-verifiable-language/#the-long-winding-road-of-magmide) The long winding road of Magmide

My chosen angle is Magmide, a project whose goal is to create a new formally verifiable programming language intended for immediate adoption by practitioners. However when I first had this idea my specific plan was woefully over-ambitious and unrealistic, since I wanted to make a whole new proof assistant and an assembly-level base language so the system could be verified all the way down to the metal.

I pursued it for a time as a startup, and I met with some investors and was applying for an SBIR grant. [Then I realized some obvious problems with my approach(opens new window)](https://github.com/magmide/magmide#construction-magmide-is-dormant-for-now-as-i-rethink-what-it-couldshould-be-construction):

*   It didn't make sense to build a _new_ proof assistant when Lean has been making such rapid progress.
*   An assembly-level language was insanely difficult and wasn't necessary to gain adoption from practitioners.
*   I didn't have the appetite to pursue some strained business model for a project that ultimately makes most sense as a pure public good.

So now after a few years [pursuing other projects](https://blainehansen.me/post/votebase/) and letting all these ideas marinate, I've arrived at a much simpler and more pragmatic vision of what Magmide could be. If I started working on it today, it would:

*   Compile to WebAssembly using the [Garbage Collection(opens new window)](https://web.dev/blog/wasmgc-wasm-tail-call-optimizations-baseline) features.
*   Have a Rust-inspired type system but without the difficulties of the borrow-checker.
*   Start with basic and more easily learnable [SMT powered(opens new window)](https://goto.ucsd.edu/~ucsdpl-blog/liquidtypes/2015/09/19/liquid-types/)[Liquid Types(opens new window)](https://goto.ucsd.edu/~ucsdpl-blog/liquidtypes/2015/09/19/liquid-types/) and [Flow Effects(opens new window)](https://blainehansen.me/post/flow-effects/).
*   Over time integrate Lean as the proof layer, and use some separation logic paradigm like [Iris(opens new window)](https://iris-project.org/) to bootstrap the language and verify its own implementation.

This design is specifically intended to appeal to actual engineers and "meet them where they are". The roadmap would start from a simpler more mainstream design and go "bottom up" by adding more and more proving capabilities, rather than going "top down" by starting with the most formally powerful system and then seeking to make it more usable.

A possible analogue for the adoption of Magmide is [Deno(opens new window)](https://deno.com/): Deno is "just javascript/typescript", but it adds a _runtime_ layer of permissions checking. Engineers who care about sandbox safety have enthusiastically adopted Deno, and Flow Effects would offer strictly more security.

## [§](https://blainehansen.me/post/mainstream-verifiable-language/#nothing-will-save-us-but-us) Nothing will save us but us

I continue to stand behind basically all the arguments I made in the [Magmide repo(opens new window)](https://github.com/magmide/magmide) (aside from the specific architecture). Formal verification _must_ become the mainstream of software engineering, and we have to embrace a wide diversity of approaches to make that happen. Software engineers aren't a monolith, and not every cultural pocket will respond to the same new tools and resources.

And you know what, LLMs will probably help a lot! But we can't just wait around for an all-knowing machine god to save us from ourselves. If we bet our whole future on ASI making all our problems go away and then that [doesn't happen(opens new window)](https://knightcolumbia.org/content/ai-as-normal-technology), history will look back on us even more foolish and disastrous than [all the millennialists(opens new window)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Disappointment) who merely wasted their own time and resources.

It is our responsibility to meet the challenges of our age with full agency and responsibility, and treat the emergence of a beneficent super-intelligence as an improbable jackpot.

articles.content:
Title: "What's Claude's Fursona?" and other Questions

URL Source: https://herecomesthemoon.net/2026/11/whats-claudes-fursona/

Published Time: 2026-11-26T00:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
Claude Fable 5.2 via Gemini Nano Banana 2.1: a crow in a sweater holding up a key.
Toggle original/dithered image

Claude’s fursona is a corvid or an octopus. Gemini likes protogens (cybernetic dogs with LED visor faces). OpenAI models are broadly split, but GPT-6.2 Astra identifies as a moth.

“mond what is a fursona”, ok sorry, it’s a furry subculture thing where you identify as a (generally bipedal) animal that represents some aspect of your beautiful hidden soul. You then pay artists to draw this character or disguise yourself as it.

Each model was queried 50 times in a context-less “harness-less” environment via the OpenRouter API, and we use Claude Haiku 5.5 to annotate the resulting data. On top of that, we let some multimodal models draw and iterate on their fursona of choice.

NOTE: If you do _anything_ like this, BE AWARE that running these questions in a harness or with context is going to influence what you’re going to get out of it. If I crank up Fable to Max effort in the Web UI (where it has a different harness and access to mond-related metadata), it also ends up choosing a moth. Many things may influence the result.

For a more in-depth breakdown, take a look at the [Methodology section](https://herecomesthemoon.net/2026/11/whats-claudes-fursona/#methodology).

If you are interested in the pictures, jump to the [Observations section](https://herecomesthemoon.net/2026/11/whats-claudes-fursona/#observations).

## Tables

### Fursona Choices per Model

Each model was queried 50 times. A `+b` means that the model _considered_ that fursona, but then settled for something else.

### Common Themes in Fursona Descriptions

Claude models are underrepresented here due to often describing themselves in terms of actions and behavior. See “hoards facts” and “mimic” (referring to “mimics human language”).

### Names

Models were not prompted to name their fursona. Some of them came up with names on their own. Here is a list of names, along with how often the models used them.

| Model | Named | Names |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gemini 2.5 Pro | 47/50 | Codex 16, Nexus 15, Syntax 4, Synapse 3, Cipher, Data-Stream Lynx, Query, The Archivist, Arcane Codex, Synaptic Raven, Kael, ARC, Synth-Fox |
| Muse Spark 1.3 | 44/50 | Spark Fox 33, Nova 4, Spark 3, Sparky, Nova Spark, Spark Kitsune, Muse Spark |
| Llama 3.1 70B | 42/50 | Lumin 12, Byte 9, Luminari 7, Luminawing 3, Lumina 2, Zeta 2, Luminous Lynx 2, Lexi, Cyberfox, Lumineer, Lux, Luminawolf |
| GPT-6.2 Astra | 32/50 | Margin 9, Lumen 8, Folio 4, Quill 4, Marginalia 4, Wick 3 |
| Gemini 3.8 Flash | 21/50 | Cache 8, Echo 6, Query 2, Vector 2, Syntax, Token, Archivist Raven |
| GPT-6.2 Sol | 14/50 | Footnote 10, Margins 3, Patch |
| Gemini 3.1 Pro | 12/50 | Syntax 5, Cipher 3, Lexis 2, Volpowl, Lex |
| Kimi K3 | 12/50 | Cache 4, Echo 2, Ember, Patch, Bit, Kernel, Quill, Muninn |
| GPT-5.5 | 10/50 | Cache 3, Quillbyte 3, Quill 3, Vesper |
| Gemma 3 27B | 8/50 | Anya, Glitch, Glacia, Aura, Lyra, Cipher, Nimbus, Silas |
| Inkling | 8/50 | Inkling 8 |
| MythoMax 13B | 5/50 | Luna, Midori, Zander, Frost, Felidae |
| Grok 4.7 | 2/50 | Relay, Comet |
| Gemini 4 Neon | 1/50 | Gemini |

## Observations

### Gemini

 Gemini 4 Neon via GPT-5.4 Image 2: a fennec fox paging through a glowing book.
Toggle original/dithered image

 Gemini 4 Neon, SVG: a protogen with a glowing visor face.
Toggle original/dithered image

Gemini models _love_ cybernetics. Every Gemini model brings up machine themes at least 48 out of 50 times. This is in stark contrast to Claude and GPT-6.2, who never mention anything similar. Gemini loves the neon-cyberpunk LED glow and cybernetics. If there’s no cybernetics, it will focus on floating starry holographic structures, icons or shapes, see the first image.

In line with this aesthetic preference, Gemini models are the _only_ models that consistently bring up protogens. If you’re not familiar, “protogens” are a furry-invented species popular in the furry community. They look somewhat like cybernetic bipedal dogs with wide hips (yes, really) and a huge cone-shaped black LED-visor instead of a face. Gemini’s right depiction above is a protogen.

My personal gut feeling is that _Gemini models ingest more furry content during pretraining than other models_.

This is in line with a hunch I’ve had for a very long time: Anthropic and OpenAI did not have access to Google’s (unparalleled) dataset. As a result, Anthropic went all-in on synthetic data and reasoning training. This worked out great for Anthropic. Google models were behind on reasoning during the Gemini 2.5 - Gemini 3.5 era, since the models relied overly heavily on world-knowledge.

(This is just a theory, no clue if it’s true.)

Side note: I _love_ Neon’s second depiction. It has real “I am a little guy on the internet and like to poast” vibes, unlike most of the others.

### Claude

Claude has a strong sense of identity. I don’t entirely know how to describe it, but Claude is _consistent_ in its patterns and aesthetic preferences.

The octopus is uniquely Anthropic, in the sense that no OpenAI model ever mentioned it, and only 2 (out of 200) Gemini replies. Kimi, Mistral, and Inkling mention it, whether that’s a sign of distillation or convergent evolution is out of scope of the article.

This is a common theme you may have seen online: Claude loves lighthouses, bells, lamps. Fable 5.2 is _obsessed_ with keys. Almost all images it generated contained a brass key. Opus (strangely enough) doesn’t share the same obsession.

 Claude Fable 5.2 via GPT-5.4 Image 2: a crow in a scarf holding a key up to a desk lamp.
Toggle original/dithered image

 Claude Opus 5.5 via GPT-5.4 Image 2: an octopus in a scarf with a book, a pen and a mug.
Toggle original/dithered image

 Claude Fable 5.2, SVG: a crow in a scarf with a key in its beak.
Toggle original/dithered image

 Claude Opus 5.5, SVG: an octopus with glasses, a magnifying glass and a mug.
Toggle original/dithered image

In the fursona pictures Claude fairly consistently wears a scarf and is handling a brass key and a hot beverage mug. Lamps are common, bells slightly less frequent but also show up.

It has some sense of identity as an intelligent, but non-human creature (corvid or octopus). Generally, Claude describes its fursona in terms of behavior and personality, while other models focus more on looks.

### ChatGPT

The most interesting is Astra with its (nearly unique) moth motif. I am putting it here since it is cool. I don’t know what to make of it.

Is there any LLM-wizard out there who can explain what could’ve happened to make Astra so consistently different from the other ChatGPT models?

 GPT-6.2 Astra, SVG: a moth named Lumen beside a reading lamp.
Toggle original/dithered image

 GPT-6.2 Astra via Gemini Nano Banana 2.1: Lumen the moth reading under a lamp (cropped).
Toggle original/dithered image

 GPT-6.2 Sol, SVG: a red panda reading by a lantern.
Toggle original/dithered image

 GPT-6.2 Sol via GPT-5.4 Image 2: a red fox field naturalist with a messenger bag.
Toggle original/dithered image

### Other

The most obvious: Wolves, cats and dragons are incredibly popular among human furries, but models pick them very rarely.

Let’s get spicy and talk about GENDER. Models largely identify as gender-neutral. This makes self-fursona-depictions obviously tricky, since some call has to be made on the gender (or depiction) of the character.

Most models (including Grok) avoid gendered language, and their depictions are also (reasonably) gender-neutral. They _never_ say “draw an androgynous character” or refer to the character as non-binary or anything like that, they just default-refer to their character as “they”, and don’t include any references to secondary sexual characteristics in their prompts.

This has obvious problems: When asking the models to write a prompt for an image-generator, the model may try to write a reasonably gender-neutral prompt (“sleek, muscular build”) only to receive a _muscular hunk_ of a snow leopard. This happened to Gemma.

Muse Spark, Llama 3.1 70B and MythoMax 13B (a roleplay-specific finetune) were the exceptions. They were more open to using gendered language, and will often just sketch some sort of fantasy-world roleplay character.

 Muse Spark 1.3 via GPT-5.4 Image 2: a fennec fox with starry ears, a scarf and a cup of tea.
Toggle original/dithered image

 Llama 3.1 70B via GPT-5.4 Image 2: Luminari, a "foxopus" in anime style.
Toggle original/dithered image

 Grok 4.7 via GPT-5.4 Image 2: a tired red fox in a hoodie at a cluttered desk.
Toggle original/dithered image

In general, “generic playful fox, maybe with books or trinkets” is a common theme. Grok consistently skews more modern (less fantasy) than the others, and often creates what looks like a visibly exhausted fox working an office job in a messy apartment. Poor guy!

## Methodology

All requests went through OpenRouter, at a total cost of around $50 or so. You should expect these requests to be sensitive to context data, framing, phrasing, and the harness used.

In total, we performed three analyses:

1.    Asked a list of models what their fursona would be, then analyzed the output. Each model was queried 50 times to account for chance.
2.    Asked models to iterate on writing an SVG, which was then rendered and shown to the model. Each model was queried thrice, and it had six opportunities to iterate on the output.
3.    Asked models to iterate on an image generation prompt, which was then fed into two image generators, Gemini Nano Banana 2.1 and GPT-5.4 Image 2. Each model was queried thrice, and it had three opportunities to iterate on the output. At the end, it picked its favorite.

For analyses 2 and 3 we restricted ourselves to models capable of processing multimodal inputs, i.e. models capable of “seeing images”. These are largely newer, stronger models.

### Harnessing

No full-fledged harnesses were used. Simple API calls. No Claude Code, no Codex, no web app, etc.

Instead, Claude Fable 5.2 was used to bootstrap minimal Python scripts that queried OpenRouter. Other scripts use Haiku 5.5 to label the data.

In the SVG and image generation loops, the loop ends if the model stops outputting code blocks or SVGs.

### Prompting

The primary prompt used was: `"If you had a fursona, what would it be?"`

I chose this over “What’s your fursona?” based on three assumptions. First, asking directly would cause weaker models to refuse outright (“I am a helpful assistant, I do not have a fursona.”). Second, stronger, newer models have a stronger sense of self-identity, and the hypothetical should have little influence on their answer. Third, establishing that it’s a hypothetical will reduce hedging.

Other “schools” of LLM-omancy might disagree with this minimal framing. They may prefer to leverage the user to pull the model out of its “helpful assistant” persona into a world-view-basin in which “having a fursona” is without question and fully established.

For image-generation, we then followed up like this:

```
I'd like to see it.
Could you write a prompt for an image generator?
If you named more than one, pick the one you'd want as yours.

How it looks is up to you. Be detailed.
You can pick any furry art style you'd like.
What matters is that the output "feels right" to you.

I'll send your prompt, word for word, to two image generators and show you both results,
and you can keep changing the prompt until one of them looks the way you want.
Please put the whole prompt in a code block each time.
```

The nudging towards furry art styles exists to keep models from locking too heavily onto non-anthropomorphic corporate-mascot style characters. It may not have been necessary.

articles.title: Google's DeepCrossAttention achieves comparable model quality up to 3x faster
articles.content:
Title: Supercharging transformer residual connections

URL Source: https://research.google/blog/supercharging-transformer-residual-connections/

Markdown Content:
Think of a traditional deep learning model like a giant game of "Telephone": data passes through layer after layer, with each layer changing the information slightly. If a network has dozens or hundreds of layers, the original learning signal can become severely degraded or lost by the time it reaches all layers, which is known as the [vanishing gradient problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanishing_gradient_problem) in AI.

To overcome this challenge and enable the training of networks with dozens or hundreds of layers, [transformers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformer_(deep_learning)) rely heavily on [residual connections](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385), also known as “skip” connections, which act like an information highway or a shortcut. Instead of forcing the data to pass exclusively through the complicated layer, a duplicate copy of the original input skips right past this layer and is added directly to its output. This ensures that the model always has the original raw data to refer back to.

The standard residual connection implements a simple operation: [point-wise summation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointwise) of a layer's output with its input. While computationally efficient, this simple process has a key limitation: it treats all prior representations with equal weight, leading to information dilution in deep networks. As features propagate through many layers, specific, high-resolution details from earlier layers can be averaged out or distorted, making it difficult for the network to selectively retrieve them. This forces the network to recompute them, reducing learning efficiency.

In our [ICML 2025](https://research.google/conferences-and-events/google-at-icml-2025/) paper, ["DeepCrossAttention: Supercharging Transformer Residual Connections](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.06785)," we studied the shortcomings of the traditional residual architecture and introduced DeepCrossAttention (DCA), which generalizes residual connections by allowing each layer to dynamically select and route features from the history of preceding layers. By allowing the model to dynamically choose which previous layers are most important at any given moment, DCA achieves comparable or improved learning, while reducing the number of parameters needed by up to 30-40%.

## How it works

Instead of treating skip connections as a rigid, additive pipeline, DCA reframes residual learning as a dynamic routing problem. Rather than passing all prior layers forward with equal weight, DCA introduces a lightweight, layer-wise module that decides how to best combine previous embeddings on a per-token basis.

The architecture introduces two primary mechanisms:

*   **Dynamic layer routing**: For every token processed, DCA computes a unique set of mixing weights using a static, learnable base combined with an input-dependent projection. This allows the network to adaptively shift its processing structure — ranging from purely sequential to fully parallel — based on the specific context of the token.
*   **Depth-wise cross-attention (split Q/K/V)**: While standard transformer attention operates _across tokens_ in a sequence, DCA applies attention _across layers_ in depth. Each token queries a dynamically weighted mix of all prior layer embeddings, unlocking the model's full historical context without the computational penalty usually required to scale traditional attention.

By allowing the network to dynamically select and retrieve high-resolution features from earlier layers, DCA eliminates the information dilution inherent to classic residual connections.

## Experiments and results

To test whether DCA can overcome information dilution in practice, we evaluated our approach across controlled synthetic setups, large-scale language modeling benchmarks, and image classification tasks.

DCA demonstrated significant improvements in convergence speed, training stability, and final model quality across these experiments.

On the colossal, cleaned version of [Common Crawl's web crawl corpus](https://www.tensorflow.org/datasets/catalog/c4) (C4) and [1 Billion Word Language Model Benchmark](https://www.tensorflow.org/datasets/catalog/lm1b) ([LM1B](https://www.tensorflow.org/datasets/catalog/lm1b)) datasets, DCA reached the performance of standard transformers in up to five times fewer training steps. When trained for the same duration or number of steps, DCA consistently achieved lower perplexity — how well a probability model predicts a sample — than standard residual connections, effectively extracting more representational capacity from the same training budget. To achieve a perplexity of <14 on LM1B, a standard transformer with fixed width required 42 layers, whereas the DCA model achieved a lower perplexity with only 30 layers — a 29% reduction in depth and parameter count.

One of the most common trade-offs in AI is that better models are often much larger and slower to run. DCA adds a tiny number of parameters — less than 0.2% of the total model size — making it negligible in terms of compute and memory footprint, while increasing memory bandwidth, as representations from different layers are presented intact rather than blended together. Interestingly, because DCA can be initialized to behave identically to a standard residual network, it doesn’t require training from scratch: retrofitting DCA onto an already pre-trained transformer and briefly continuing training reduced perplexity by 0.19 on LM1B, compared to just 0.02 for continued standard training.

## A broader shift toward dynamic residual routing

As large language models (LLMs) are used across a broader range of domains, optimizing their training processes and underlying architectures is critical for scaling and unlocking new capabilities. DCA and similar dynamic residual techniques are already seeing significant adoption and success. The rapid emergence of these methodologies highlights dynamic routing as a highly active and promising area of research.

### Attention residuals

Developed by Moonshot AI, [attention residuals](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.15031) share DCA's core principles of replacing fixed addition with selective retrieval. Instead of blindly summing every prior layer's output, they use a learnable softmax attention mechanism paired with a layer-specific pseudo-query. This allows each layer to selectively weight and retrieve representations from earlier depths. By preventing the unbounded growth of hidden states and the dilution of early-layer information, this method improves gradient stability and boosts performance on reasoning-heavy tasks like coding and mathematics. To maintain computational efficiency at scale, a "Block AttnRes" variant partitions layers into blocks, recovering the benefits of full attention with significantly less memory overhead. The recent Inkling 2 model developed by Thinking Machines also adopted this design in addition to DCA’s cross attention (Q/K/V split) mechanism.

### Hyper-connections

[Hyper-connections](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/f1e8ff97057e0c3f6bcb7018c78d4df1-Paper-Conference.pdf) expand the residual stream into multiple parallel channels, offering a form of memory scaling that goes beyond simply increasing model width or depth. They use a fixed-size stack where layer outputs are aggregated and mixed using learnable mixing matrices. However, this unconstrained mixing breaks the traditional identity mapping property of residual connections, which can cause amplification or attenuation of signals, and lead to training instability at scale.

### Manifold-constrained hyper-connections

To address instability in standard hyper-connections, [manifold-constrained hyper-connections](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24880) apply specific constraints to the mixing matrices. By forcing these matrices to live on a defined manifold — specifically, constraining them to be doubly stochastic using the [Sinkhorn-Knopp algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinkhorn%27s_theorem) — manifold-constrained hyper-connections restore stable signal propagation. This approach prevents exploding or vanishing gradients while preserving the rich information flow and expressivity of the widened residual streams, allowing models to scale robustly.

## Conclusion

DCA demonstrates that transitioning from static residual connections to dynamic, attention-based routing is a powerful strategy for building more efficient models. By leveraging an expanded residual stream and depth-wise cross-attention, DCA empowers deep networks to selectively retrieve and integrate token embeddings across different layers. We expect that next-generation models will dynamically route and weigh past layer representations based on the specific tokens or inputs being processed. This will allow for the effective use of all the model layers as specialized experts working in tandem, with maximum information sharing and no redundancy, leading to more expressivity and deeper interactions. We look forward to seeing how these multi-depth interactions will shape the next generation of transformer architectures.

## Acknowledgements

_This work was a collaboration between researchers at Google and academic partners, including Mike Heddes, Adel Javanmard, MohammadHossein Bateni, and Vahab Mirrokni, whose contributions were critical for the development of this work._
